questions.stem: A team lead asks Claude for 25 playful name ideas for an internal quarterly hackathon. She plans to paste the list into the team chat so people can vote on a favorite. A colleague suggests sending the list to Legal and Brand for formal review first, just to be safe. What is the MOST appropriate level of review?

options.text: Send the list to Legal and Brand for formal sign-off, because any AI-generated text shared with colleagues needs expert approval.
Ask Claude to confirm that none of the names could cause problems, and treat its answer as the review.
Read the list herself, drop anything that seems off or inappropriate for the team, and post it for the vote.
Avoid using Claude for this, since a naming exercise is something the team should brainstorm without AI help.

questions.explanation: Review should be **proportionate to the stakes**. This is an internal, low-risk, easily reversible brainstorm: no customers, no regulated content, no decisions about people. A quick self-check by the person posting it (reading it and removing anything unsuitable) is enough. The exam rewards matching the review to the risk, not escalating everything.

whyWrong.A: Formal expert sign-off for an internal vote on hackathon names wastes reviewer time. Over-review is a trap too: proportionate review is the goal.
whyWrong.B: Claude checking its own output is not a review, and handing the final call to it skips the simple human read that this low-stakes task needs.
whyWrong.D: Brainstorming is a strong use of Claude. Dropping it entirely is an overreaction when a quick read handles the small risk.

questions.mindset: Match review effort to stakes: low-risk internal drafts need a self-check, not a committee.

questions.stem: A marketing manager at a software company uses Claude to draft answers to a prospective enterprise customer's 60-question security questionnaire. The answers cover encryption, data retention and incident response, and the customer will rely on them in its vendor decision. She reads the draft and it sounds convincing to her. Before it goes to the customer, which review step is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Have the company's security or IT owner check each technical answer against the actual controls before it is sent.
Have a senior copy editor in marketing polish the answers so that they read consistently and professionally.
Ask Claude to reread its answers and list any it is unsure about, then send the ones it marks as confident.
Send the answers, since she has already read them closely and they match how the company describes itself.

questions.explanation: A meaningful review needs a reviewer who can **judge the content**. Security questionnaire answers are external, technical claims that a customer will rely on, and possibly hold the company to. The marketing manager cannot verify encryption or retention details herself, so the owner of those facts (security or IT) must confirm each answer against how the systems really work.

whyWrong.B: Copy editing improves wording but cannot catch a wrong technical claim. A reviewer without the expertise turns review into a formality.
whyWrong.C: Claude's self-reported confidence is not evidence. It can be confidently wrong about the company's real controls, which it never saw.
whyWrong.D: Sounding right to a non-expert is exactly the failure mode. 'Convincing' is not 'verified', and the stakes here are external and contractual.

questions.mindset: The reviewer must be able to judge the content: route technical claims to the owner of the facts.

questions.stem: An operations coordinator uses Claude to turn the company's travel and expense policy into a 20-question FAQ for the intranet. Every new hire (about 400 people a year) will be pointed to it, and many will rely on it instead of the full policy. The draft includes daily meal limits, mileage rates and approval thresholds. Which TWO steps are MOST appropriate before publishing? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to append a confidence score to each answer so readers know which answers to double-check themselves.
Check every limit, rate and threshold in the FAQ against the current official policy document, line by line.
Publish it now and correct any errors as employees report them, since the FAQ can be updated at any time.
Add a line at the top saying the FAQ was generated with AI and may contain mistakes, so readers stay cautious.
Have the policy owner in Finance review and approve the FAQ once before it goes live on the intranet.

questions.explanation: Content that will be **reused many times** multiplies any error: one wrong meal limit misleads hundreds of people. That raises the review level even though the content is internal. The right steps are to **verify the specific figures against the authoritative source** (the current policy) and to have the **owner of that source of truth** approve it. After that, the FAQ can be reused safely.

whyWrong.A: Self-reported confidence scores are not a reliable accuracy signal, and they push the checking work onto 400 readers instead of doing it once.
whyWrong.C: Waiting for complaints means employees have already acted on wrong numbers, and some errors will never be reported at all.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer does not make anything accurate. It shifts responsibility to readers rather than fixing the content.

questions.mindset: Reuse multiplies risk: verify once against the source and get owner approval before something becomes a template.

questions.stem: A procurement analyst asks Claude what value threshold triggers a formal customs declaration for a shipment of samples to another country. She asks the same question in a new chat later that day to double-check and gets a different figure. She needs the right answer for a shipment leaving this week. What should she do NEXT?

options.text: Use the figure from the second chat, since Claude had more chances to reason about the question the second time.
Ask in a third chat and use whichever figure appears in two of the three answers as the deciding vote.
Paste both answers into one chat and ask Claude to explain which one is correct and why the other is wrong.
Treat both figures as unverified and confirm the threshold with the official customs authority or the company's freight broker.

questions.explanation: When different runs give **different facts**, that inconsistency is itself a signal that Claude is not reliably grounded on this point, and regulatory thresholds also change over time. Neither figure should be used until it is confirmed against an **authoritative source** (the customs authority) or a qualified party (the freight broker). With a real shipment and possible penalties at stake, outside verification is required.

whyWrong.A: A later answer is not more reliable just because it came second. Both came from the same unverified source.
whyWrong.B: A majority vote of unverified answers is still unverified. Consistency between runs does not prove the figure is current or correct.
whyWrong.C: Asking Claude to judge between its own answers keeps the check inside the same source. It may confidently justify the wrong one.

questions.mindset: Conflicting answers across runs mean 'go to the authoritative source', not 'ask again'.

questions.stem: After a six-hour service outage, a customer support lead uses Claude to draft an apology email that will go to all 12,000 customers through the company's email platform. The draft states that every affected customer will receive a credit equal to one week of service, applied automatically. Once sent, the email cannot be recalled. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate before sending? Choose TWO.

options.text: Confirm with the finance or billing owner that the credit is approved, including the amount and how it will be applied.
Regenerate the email several times and send whichever version describes the credit most consistently.
Add a footer stating the message was drafted with AI assistance, so customers understand any errors in it.
Have the communications or support manager who owns customer messaging approve the final text before release.
Ask Claude to review the email for accuracy and send it once Claude confirms nothing needs changing.

questions.explanation: This output is **external, irreversible and high-reach**, and it makes a **financial commitment**. Two checks fit the risk: verify the specific commitment (the credit) with the person who owns that decision, and have the owner of customer communications approve the final message. Claude still saves time by drafting, but people sign off before anything this consequential leaves the building.

whyWrong.B: Consistent wording across regenerations proves nothing about whether finance actually approved a one-week credit.
whyWrong.C: A disclosure footer does not stop a wrong promise from reaching 12,000 people. It is not a substitute for checking.
whyWrong.E: Claude reviewing its own draft is not independent verification, and it has no way to know what credit the business approved.

questions.mindset: Irreversible, mass-audience messages with commitments need the commitment verified and the message approved by its owner.

questions.stem: A nonprofit volunteer coordinator asks Claude to write a one-page handout on preventing heat illness for volunteers working outdoors at a summer event. It covers warning signs, how much water to drink and when to call emergency services. The draft looks thorough and clear. What is the MOST appropriate step before printing it for volunteers?

options.text: Print it as written, since heat safety is common knowledge and Claude's draft covers the main points well.
Have someone qualified, such as the event's first-aid lead or a health professional, review the guidance first.
Ask Claude to add a note telling volunteers to consult a doctor, then print the handout without further checks.
Shorten the handout to just the emergency phone number so that there is no health guidance that could be wrong.

questions.explanation: **Health and safety information** that people will act on is a clear trigger for human review: a wrong hydration amount or a missed warning sign could cause real harm. The right move is to keep Claude's useful draft and have a **qualified person** confirm it before distribution.

whyWrong.A: Looking thorough is not the same as being accurate. Safety guidance that people will act on needs a qualified check, not an assumption.
whyWrong.C: A 'consult a doctor' note shifts responsibility to volunteers who will be in the field, not at a clinic. It does not verify the content.
whyWrong.D: Removing the useful guidance is an overreaction that leaves volunteers less safe. Review fixes the risk; deletion just discards the value.

questions.mindset: If people could be harmed by acting on it, a qualified human checks it first.

questions.stem: A department manager has a year of peer feedback for each of her eight direct reports. She asks Claude to summarize each person's feedback and suggest a performance rating (1 to 5) for each, which feeds into pay decisions. Claude's summaries read well and the suggested ratings seem reasonable. With the least risk of an unfair outcome, how should she use this output?

options.text: Submit Claude's suggested ratings, since an AI applies the same standard to everyone and avoids her own personal bias.
Ask Claude to remove any biased wording from the summaries, then submit the ratings it suggested unchanged.
Stop using Claude for performance work, and write every summary and rating by hand from the raw feedback.
Use the summaries as a starting point, check them against the raw feedback, and decide and own each rating herself.

questions.explanation: Ratings that drive pay are **decisions about people**, which call for human judgment and accountability. Claude can help organize a large volume of feedback, but the manager must check the summaries against the source (summaries can drop context or overweight a single comment) and make and own each rating herself. Her organization's normal calibration process still applies.

whyWrong.A: AI output is not automatically neutral. Summaries can inherit or amplify bias in the source comments, and the accountability stays with the manager.
whyWrong.B: Cleaning up wording treats the symptom. The ratings would still be Claude's decision, which is the step that needs a human.
whyWrong.C: This overreacts. Claude can save real time organizing feedback, provided a human verifies it and makes the call.

questions.mindset: Claude can organize the evidence; a person makes and owns decisions about people.

questions.stem: A bid manager is assembling a 40-page response to a public-sector tender. About 30 pages are company boilerplate copied from a library that Legal already approved this year. Claude drafted the remaining sections: a new pricing schedule, a service-level commitment with penalty terms, and a project timeline. The deadline is in two days and reviewers are scarce. Which review approach is MOST effective?

options.text: Send the new pricing to Finance and the service-level and penalty terms to Legal, and have the delivery lead check the timeline.
Have one reviewer read the entire 40 pages from start to finish so that nothing in the response goes unchecked.
Skip formal review, because most of the document is pre-approved and the deadline leaves too little time for it.
Ask Claude to compare its new sections with the approved boilerplate and flag any inconsistencies as the final check.

questions.explanation: Good review is **targeted**. The pre-approved boilerplate carries little new risk; the new Claude-drafted sections carry contractual and financial commitments. Routing each high-risk section to the person qualified to judge it (Finance for pricing, Legal for penalties, delivery for the timeline) puts scarce reviewer time where errors would be most costly, and it fits the deadline.

whyWrong.B: A single generalist reading 40 pages spreads effort thin and probably lacks the expertise to judge both pricing and penalty clauses.
whyWrong.C: Deadline pressure does not remove the need to check new contractual and pricing commitments. Those are the riskiest parts.
whyWrong.D: Consistency with boilerplate does not show the prices or penalties are right. Claude checking its own sections is not expert sign-off.

questions.mindset: Spend review where the new risk is: route each high-stakes section to the expert who can judge it.

questions.stem: A strategy associate asks Claude to draft a briefing for the leadership team on a competitor's recent moves. Most of the briefing draws on the analyst reports she uploaded. In one paragraph, however, Claude writes that the competitor 'may have completed an acquisition of a regional distributor earlier this year, though I could not confirm this from the provided materials.' Leadership may act on that point. What is the MOST appropriate way to handle that paragraph?

options.text: Remove the hedging phrase so the briefing reads with confidence, since leadership prefers clear statements.
Ask Claude to rewrite the paragraph more confidently, using what it knows about the competitor's strategy.
Verify the acquisition against a reliable source such as a press release or filing, then state it or drop it.
Delete the whole briefing and start over, because one uncertain claim means the rest of it cannot be trusted.

questions.explanation: When Claude **signals uncertainty** or makes a claim that is **not in your source material**, that point needs additional verification, especially when leaders may act on it. Confirm the claim against an authoritative source (a press release, regulatory filing or reputable news report). If it is confirmed, state it with the source; if not, leave it out or clearly label it as unconfirmed.

whyWrong.A: Deleting the hedge turns an unverified claim into an apparent fact, which hides the very warning that should prompt a check.
whyWrong.B: Asking for more confidence pushes Claude to sound surer without adding any evidence. That raises the risk of a hallucinated detail.
whyWrong.D: The rest of the briefing is grounded in the uploaded reports. Discarding all of it overreacts to one claim that can be checked.

questions.mindset: Claude's own hedges and unsourced claims are flags: verify them, never polish them away.

questions.stem: An office manager is organizing travel for six employees attending a conference abroad next month. She asks Claude which entry visa or travel authorization each employee needs, based on their nationalities. Claude gives a clear, country-by-country answer. What should she do before telling the employees what to apply for?

options.text: Forward Claude's answer to the employees, since entry requirements are published widely and Claude covers them well.
Confirm each requirement on the destination country's official government site or with the company's travel provider.
Ask Claude to repeat the answer in a table and recheck it, then send that table to the employees.
Tell each employee to work out their own entry requirements, since AI should not be used for travel planning.

questions.explanation: Entry requirements are **fast-changing**, rules-based facts that people will act on, and a mistake could leave an employee unable to travel. Claude's knowledge may be out of date. Confirm each requirement with the **authoritative source** (the destination government's official site) or a qualified travel provider before employees apply.

whyWrong.A: Recent or changing rules are exactly where Claude may be outdated, and the cost of a mistake falls on the traveler.
whyWrong.C: Reformatting and rechecking in the same chat does not bring in an authoritative source. A neat table can still be wrong.
whyWrong.D: Claude can still help her organize the task. Pushing all the work onto each employee overreacts instead of adding a quick check.

questions.mindset: Recent or changing rules that people will act on must be confirmed at the official source.

questions.stem: A consulting team lead sets up a Claude Project that the team will use every week to draft client proposals. She wants to make sure that, every time, the parts of each draft that need expert checking are reviewed before it reaches a client, without slowing down the routine sections. Which setup is MOST effective?

options.text: Add a project instruction telling Claude to be fully accurate and never include figures that it is not sure about.
Upload past winning proposals as project knowledge, so that new drafts follow approved wording and need no review.
Have each consultant ask Claude at the end of each draft whether it is ready to send to the client, and follow its answer.
Instruct Claude to tag pricing, legal and delivery commitments for review, and add a team rule naming who signs off each tag.

questions.explanation: Review works best when it is **built into the workflow**. A Project can carry instructions that apply to its chats, so asking Claude to **flag** high-risk content (pricing, legal terms, delivery commitments) makes reviewers' jobs faster and more consistent across every draft. The flags help the humans; they do not replace them. Pairing them with a team rule that names the reviewer for each type of flag makes sure the right person checks those parts every time.

whyWrong.A: Telling Claude to 'be accurate' does not make it reliably accurate. A prompt instruction cannot replace a human check on client commitments.
whyWrong.B: Good reference material improves drafts, but new prices and commitments still change per client and still need checking.
whyWrong.C: Letting Claude decide whether its own draft is ready removes the human gate that client-facing commitments need.

questions.mindset: Build review into the workflow: Claude flags, named humans sign off.

questions.stem: A management consultant uses Claude to build a three-year revenue forecast from a client's historical sales spreadsheet. The forecast will appear in a board presentation that the client uses to decide whether to open two new locations. To save time, he plans to add the note 'Prepared with AI assistance; figures may contain errors' and send it. Which TWO steps would BEST replace that plan? Choose TWO.

options.text: Rerun the forecast with the most capable Claude model available, since a stronger model makes calculation errors less likely.
Keep the AI note but make it more prominent, placing it on the first slide so the board sees it before the figures.
Reconcile the forecast's starting figures and growth assumptions against the client's source spreadsheet.
Ask Claude to explain its reasoning step by step, and treat a clear explanation as confirmation that the numbers are right.
Have a qualified colleague, such as the engagement's finance lead, review the model and assumptions before it goes out.

questions.explanation: This is a **financial output that will drive a major decision** by an external client, which is a clear trigger for qualified human review. A disclaimer shifts risk to the reader instead of reducing it. The right replacement is to **verify the numbers against the source data** and have a **qualified reviewer** check the model and its assumptions before release.

whyWrong.A: A bigger model can still misread data or make unrealistic assumptions. Model choice is not a substitute for verification.
whyWrong.B: Making the disclaimer bigger is still a disclaimer. It does not catch a single wrong number.
whyWrong.D: A fluent explanation can make wrong numbers look right. Claude's reasoning about its own work is not independent verification.

questions.mindset: A disclaimer is not a review: verify the numbers and get a qualified sign-off.

questions.stem: A non-technical project manager is writing a plan to move her team's customer records from an old system to a new one. She asks Claude how to do the migration, and it recommends a specific approach with steps for exporting, transforming and importing the data. The plan goes to the steering committee on Friday. She cannot judge whether the approach is sound. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Have the technical lead or a developer review the approach before it is presented as the plan to the committee.
Include the approach as written, since Claude's technical recommendations are usually reliable for routine work.
Ask Claude to list the risks of its own approach, and add that list to the plan as evidence it has been checked.
Remove the migration approach from the plan entirely and leave that section blank until a later meeting.

questions.explanation: When you **cannot verify a claim yourself**, the output needs review by someone who can. A data migration recommendation is technical and hard to reverse if done badly. Associates are expected to recognize where their role stops and hand technical decisions to developers or architects. Claude's draft is still useful as a starting point for the technical lead.

whyWrong.B: 'Usually reliable' is not verification, and a migration error affects customer records. That is high stakes.
whyWrong.C: Claude critiquing its own plan is useful input but not an independent check. It cannot stand in for a qualified reviewer.
whyWrong.D: Leaving the section blank wastes Claude's useful draft. Routing it to the right reviewer keeps both its value and the schedule.

questions.mindset: If you can't judge it, route it to someone who can: know where the Associate role stops.

questions.stem: A product manager at an appliance maker uses Claude to translate a product safety notice (warning customers to stop using a heater model until a part is replaced) from English into Spanish for customers in Latin America. She doesn't speak Spanish. To check the translation, she plans to ask Claude to translate the Spanish back into English and compare it with the original. What is the MOST reliable way to confirm the translation before it is published?

options.text: Do the back-translation in a new chat, so that the check is not influenced by the earlier conversation's context.
Run the back-translation with a more capable model, then publish if the English matches the original closely.
Have a fluent, qualified Spanish reviewer, ideally familiar with the regional market, check it before release.
Publish the Spanish version along with the English original, so readers can refer to the English if unsure.

questions.explanation: A **safety notice** that customers will act on is high stakes, and the product manager **cannot judge the output herself**. Back-translation by the same kind of system is a weak check: it can smooth over wrong terms, an unclear instruction or a regional usage that would confuse readers. A **qualified human reviewer** fluent in the target language is the reliable control.

whyWrong.A: A fresh chat removes some context, but it is still Claude checking Claude. It may miss errors that a fluent reader would catch at once.
whyWrong.B: A stronger model is a tempting disguise for the same weak check. Close English wording does not prove the Spanish is clear for local readers.
whyWrong.D: Many customers may not read English. Shifting the burden to them does not make a safety instruction reliable.

questions.mindset: When you can't read the output and people's safety depends on it, a qualified human checks it, not another AI pass.

questions.stem: A support team lead is rolling out Claude to draft replies to customer emails. Agents will read each draft and send it themselves. She wants a short rule saying which drafts must go to a specialist before sending, so that review effort goes where the risk is without slowing every reply down. Which TWO criteria BEST belong in that rule? Choose TWO.

options.text: Any draft longer than about 200 words, because longer replies contain more sentences that could be wrong.
Any draft that commits to a refund, policy exception or compensation beyond what the agent is authorized to give.
Any draft whose tone seems less warm than the team's style guide, so the brand voice stays consistent.
Any draft that mentions possible legal action, a data or privacy concern, or a regulator complaint.
Any draft for a customer who has written in more than twice before, since repeat contacts are more frustrated.

questions.explanation: Escalation criteria should track **stakes**, not surface features. Drafts that make **commitments beyond the agent's authority** (money, exceptions) and drafts that touch **legal, privacy or regulatory** issues carry consequences that a specialist must judge. Routine replies can stay with the agent's own read, which keeps the workflow fast while protecting the cases that matter.

whyWrong.A: Length is a poor proxy for risk. A two-line reply promising a refund is riskier than a long how-to answer.
whyWrong.C: Tone matters, but the agent can fix it during their own read. It doesn't need specialist escalation.
whyWrong.E: Repeat contact may call for extra care, but it is not by itself a legal, financial or privacy risk that needs a specialist.

questions.mindset: Escalate on consequences (commitments, legal, privacy), not on surface features like length or tone.
